sections.explanation: Direct proportionality means y=kx with fixed k: doubling x doubles y. Inverse proportionality means y=k/x, for non-zero x: doubling x halves y. Inverse-square dependence means y=k/x²: doubling x divides y by four. These statements require other parameters to remain fixed. “Increases with” does not by itself mean direct proportionality; y=x+5 increases with x but does not preserve y/x.
sections.worked: For supplied travel time t=d/v at fixed d, replacing v by 3v gives t/3. At fixed v, replacing d by 3d gives 3t. For supplied intensity I=k/r², increasing r from 2 to 6 multiplies distance by 3 and intensity by 1/9.

sections.explanation: Dimensions identify kinds of quantity: write L for length and T for time. Speed has dimensions L/T; area has L². Terms added or equated must have compatible dimensions. A dimensionless numerical constant does not change dimensions. Dimensional compatibility is necessary for a physical equation written in ordinary quantities, but it cannot determine every numerical coefficient or establish a physical law.
sections.worked: The model d=vt is dimensionally compatible because(L/T)T=L. So is d=2vt. Dimensions cannot choose between them. But d=v+t attempts to add L/T to T, so it is incompatible. This is a structural error before any values are substituted.

sections.explanation: Use code to evaluate stated scenarios after predicting their ratio. This separates understanding of the dependence from arithmetic execution. Name the fixed inputs explicitly. Compare outputs through a ratio as well as their individual values. Keep the original scenario visible so that the ratio has a clearly defined reference.
sections.worked: For distance 120 m, speeds 4 and 12 m/s give times 30 and 10 s. The speed ratio is 3 and the time ratio is 1/3. Agreement with this prediction is a useful check, but does not validate the physical assumptions of the model.
tasks: Type both time calculations using named inputs.

feedback: 25 and 6.25; the latter is one quarter.
It checks the numeric evaluation against a scaling prediction; it does not demonstrate that a real source obeys this law.

time_b_s = distance_m / 12
print(time_a_s)

sections.explanation: A model makes a conditional prediction. Inverse-square examples here assume a fixed source and a supplied law; we do not derive that law or infer its universal validity. Keep the difference between a predicted ratio and an observed result visible. An observation would require data and information about how it was obtained.
sections.worked: A supplied model gives I=80 at r=3 in consistent units. At r=9, the distance triples and the model predicts I=80/9≈8.89. The exact ratio 1/9 is clearer than the rounded output. Changing the source strength at the same time would invalidate this particular comparison.

sections.explanation: Use the first 30 minutes of this section to review your Unit 1 and Unit 2 work. Locate one corrected calculation, one unit conversion and one scaling explanation. Then attempt iCMA 41 using its dedicated assessment page. The assessment occupies the remaining 60 minutes already allocated here; it is not additional homework. Follow its instructions about permitted tools and submission. A self-check is useful practice, but a saved formal attempt must go through the submission route.
sections.worked: A useful readiness explanation is: “In a centimetre-squared to metre-squared conversion I square the length factor because area contains two length factors.” A rule recalled without its reason is a prompt to revisit the diagram, not a reason to panic.
